newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian PM attacks anti-Hanson protests.
newsitem.headline: Australian PM attacks anti-Hanson protests.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard on Thursday condemned violent protests against race row politician Pauline Hanson and her One Nation party as counter-productive.
Howard said the rowdy protests at two launches of the One Nation party earlier this week only served to highlight Hanson's extremist views on immigration and Aborigines.
"Their (the protesters') behaviour is worse than the behaviour of some of the people they attack," said Howard in an interview on a Sydney radio station.
"I think those demonstrations at her rallies are counter-productive. If they think they are damaging the cause against which they're demonstrating, they're wrong," he said.
"These thugs who are trying to bust up all these meetings are really helping her, they're not harming her."
Police said a small group of militant protesters turned violent at a One Nation meeting in the Victorian rural town of Dandenong on Monday night.
The protesters threw urine-filled balloons and eggs and attacked pro-Hanson supporters, leaving one elderly man with a fractured skull.

Howard has been criticised by former prime ministers, human rights officials and ethnic leaders for not strongly repudiating Hanson and her views and allowing the current bitter race debate to continue.

Hanson, an independent who won office at the last election in March 1996, stands on an anti-immigration platform and has criticised Aboriginal welfare. Hanson sparked the race debate in September last year when she said Australia was in danger of being swamped by Asians.

Asians currently make up only 4.8 percent of Australia's 18 million population and are expected to make up 7.5 percent of the population in the next 30 years, according to official immigration statistics.
Hanson has vowed to continue rallying party support for her newly registered party, despite increasingly violent protests.
Recent opinion polls put support for Hanson at between six and 10 percent.
